analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to give or accept gifts rewarding state and local officials over public business.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in September 2024 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close a gap in federal anti-corruption law. Under current law, a contractor who pays a state or local official before a favorable decision can be charged with bribery, but a payment made after the official has already steered a contract — a "gratuity" — is not a federal crime (the Supreme Court narrowed this in its 2024 Snyder v. United States ruling). The bill would make it a crime, punishable by up to 2 years in prison, to give or accept anything of value intended to reward an official in connection with a public transaction worth $5,000 or more.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and residents of states, cities, and towns, whose officials could no longer be legally rewarded with gifts for steering contracts and other public business; and honest contractors, who would compete on the merits rather than against firms willing to give officials gifts after the fact.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to 2 years in prison and a fine, for anyone to give or accept anything of value intended to reward a state, local, or tribal official or government agent in connection with a business transaction worth $5,000 or more [S2].

It closes the 'gratuity' gap: before this change, only a payment made before an official act (a bribe) was covered by this federal statute, while a reward paid after the official had already delivered the favor could escape prosecution [S2].

It applies the same rules to both sides — the official who solicits or accepts the reward and the person who gives it — so prosecutors no longer have to prove a payment was agreed to in advance to reach the giver [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and individuals who currently reward state and local officials with gifts after favorable decisions, and the officials who accept those rewards — both would face fines and up to 2 years in prison. Some officials and businesses might also face compliance costs to avoid even the appearance of a prohibited gift.
analysis.who_pays_short: Officials and businesses trading gifts for favors

drawbacks.text: The prohibition only covers transactions worth $5,000 or more and, under the existing statute it amends, only where federal funds are involved, so smaller-scale gift-giving and purely local programs would remain outside federal law [S2].
The maximum penalty of 2 years is lighter than what many state bribery laws carry, which critics could argue limits the deterrence for the largest deals [S2].

Extending federal criminal law further into state and local government conduct raises a federalism objection — that states should police their own officials' ethics — which is a standard argument against federalizing local corruption cases [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — restoring the ability to prosecute officials who accept rewards for steering public money, after a 2024 Supreme Court decision removed that tool — is concrete and directly protects public funds. The main costs are the limits built in: the $5,000 transaction threshold, the restriction to federally funded programs, and a 2-year maximum sentence keep the law narrow. On balance it is a targeted anti-corruption fix, though a narrow one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2024 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, with Senators Warren, Whitehouse, and Welch as cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the full Senate never considered it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses and public officials who benefit from the status quo — the ability to reward officials with gifts after favorable decisions without federal criminal exposure — are better off, because the gap left by the Supreme Court's 2024 Snyder ruling remains open. No one else is better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gift-giving contractors and the officials they reward

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Peter Welch

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by a Democrat in this Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or reported it out, keeping it from any Senate action.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.role: 49 of 100 Senate seats; none of the 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator signed on, leaving the bill with no bipartisan base that might have moved it.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters were Democrats — the sponsor plus 3 of the 48 Senate Democrats — and none of the 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored, so the bill never had the bipartisan support needed to move through committee in the closing months of a Congress.

industries.industry: Government contractors and businesses seeking state and local contracts
industries.note: Firms that reward officials with gifts after winning or steering a public deal would face federal fines and prison terms. The industry's interest in keeping the current gap runs against taxpayers, who foot the bill for favoritism in public contracting.

industries.industry: State, local, and tribal government officials
industries.note: Officials could no longer accept things of value as rewards for official decisions on public business without federal criminal exposure. The public's interest is in officials whose decisions are not for sale.
